activity_context.topic_title: The Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

feedback.problem: Let $f(x)={x}^{2}+5x+1.$ Find ${g}^{′}(5)$ given the function is defined by $g(x)={\int }_{x}^{7}f(t)\,\text{d}t.$
feedback.worked_solution:
In this example, the variable limit $x$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of definite integrals, we can write

$$
g(x)={\int }_{x}^{7}({t}^{2}+5t+1)\,\text{d}t=-{\int }_{7}^{x}({t}^{2}+5t+1)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, by FTC II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{x}^{7}({t}^{2}+5t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{7}^{x}({t}^{2}+5t+1)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{7}^{x}({t}^{2}+5t+1)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+5x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the value of ${g}^{′}(5),$ we substitute $x=5$ in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(5) & =-({5}^{2}+5\cdot 5+1) \\  & =-(25+25+1) \\  & =-51\end{aligned}
$$
